title: Karmic Tail 6-17-11 in the Destiny Matrix: a Ruined Talent, the Water of Life for Nothing and a Lion on a Chain of Flowers

seo.title: 6-17-11 Karmic Tail in the Destiny Matrix: The Ruined Talent
seo.description: 6-17-11: a gift that was never lost, only drained away for nothing. The Lovers, the Star and Strength, Death at the centre, a date check, eight practices.

short: 6-17-11 is the karmic tail that popular destiny matrix readings call the "Ruined Talent". The name is misleading: it sounds like a story about someone who was never given any ability, or who lacked the grit to use it. The cards say something else. In the middle of the tail stands the Star — a woman pouring water from two jugs, the card of the gift. The gift is there. The tail's scenario is about where it drains away. The entry is the Lovers (6): talent appears in the eyes of another person — the one who noticed it, praised it, loved it, or forced a choice. The Star (17) keeps the loop going: the gift pours onto someone else's land, is handed out for free and lives in the future tense, as hope. At the root stands Strength (11): a woman leading a lion on a chain of flowers. Her task is to take her own gift in hand and endure the long work without which it stays a promise. And at the centre of the matrix, for nearly everyone with this tail, stands Death — a card that in the Marseille deck does not even have a name.

sections.h2: How to find the 6-17-11 tail from a date of birth
paragraphs: The tail depends entirely on the sum of the first three numbers of the matrix. For 6-17-11 there are four such sums, and the check takes less than a minute.

ol: **Day arcanum** — the day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 25 → 7, 29 → 11, 31 → 4.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If the result is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1985 → 23 → 5, 1990 → 19, 2007 → 9.

paragraphs: Now add the three numbers. **A sum of 38, 47 or 56 gives 6-17-11 with Death at the centre. A sum of 11 gives the same tail with the Fool at the centre.** Any other sum gives a different tail.

ul: 01.01.2007: 1 + 1 + 9 = **11** → 6-17-11 with the Fool at the centre.
05.05.1990: 5 + 5 + 19 = 29 → not this one. That is 15-8-11: Strength is at the root there too, but the entry and the mechanism are different.

paragraphs: Why this works. The tail is the three points of the chart's lower ray: M next to the centre, N in the middle, D in the lower corner. All four sums fold into 11 (3 + 8, 4 + 7, 5 + 6, and 11 stays itself) — that is the root D. Then the method adds the root to the sum to get the centre, gets the entry from the centre, and the middle from the entry:

With a sum of 11 the centre comes out differently: 11 + 11 = 22, the Fool. But the entry is still the Lovers: 11 + 22 = 33 → 6. With a sum of 29 the centre becomes 4 — and the tail turns into 15-8-11. So of the five sums that fold into 11, four give 6-17-11 and one gives its neighbour.

A sum of 56 is the largest possible: the 22nd day, December and a year whose digits add up to 22. Since 1900 there have been exactly seven such dates — 22 December of 1939, 1948, 1957, 1966, 1975, 1984 and 1993.
The same arithmetic yields a few facts you will rarely find anywhere else:

ul: **About one person in 22 gets it.** Among people born in 1940–2012, 6-17-11 comes up in 4.6% of cases — eighth place out of 26 possible tails.

**It thins out with every generation.** Among people born in the 1930s–1950s it is one in 18; in the 1990s, one in 24; in the 2000s, already one in 41. After 2000 the year arcanum became small (from 2 to 10), and reaching 38 or 47 became harder.

**The generation of the 2000s has a different centre.** Before 2000 the Fool stands at the centre for one owner of the tail in twenty. After 2000, for more than half: small sums more often come to exactly 11.
**December has 2.4 times as many dates with this tail as February.** The higher the month number, the easier it is to reach 38.

paragraphs: Popular readings explain the name with a legend about a past life. The soul supposedly received a bright gift — creative, spiritual, human — and never put it to work. The legend comes in several versions. It gave up its calling for a steady income or for family. The gift went to its head, and pride ended in a fall. It could not stand the mockery and criticism, and hid the gift away. One retelling even adds love spells. The name wanders too: "Ruined", "Destroyed", "Unrealised Talent" (in Russian Zagublenny, Pogublenny, Nerealizovanny talant), and one forum list of compatibility tails gives the same set of numbers the name "Wicked Love".
The legend cannot be checked: the numbers say nothing about past lives. But the name has supports that can be checked. There are two, and the first lies in the word itself.

The word "talent" in the sense of "ability" comes from the parable in the Gospel (Matthew 25:14–30). A master, before a journey, hands his servants talents — the name of a large measure of silver, about 26 kilograms. Two put the money to work and double it. The third buries his, and when the master returns he explains: "And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine." The talent is taken from him. Hence the old phrase "to bury one's talent" — and hence the central question of this tail. The servant did not lose the money or squander it. He was afraid, and never put it to use.

The second support is in the cards. Open Waite's divinatory list for the Star, the middle card of the tail. The first words there are "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment". Only after them: "another reading says—hope and bright prospects". For the reversed Star Waite gives "Arrogance, haughtiness, impotence". A calculated number in the matrix is never reversed, but these lists show which shadows interpreters saw in the card. And every plot of the legend fits into them. The gift is lost, taken, abandoned — that is giving up the calling. Arrogance and haughtiness — the pride that went to the head. Impotence — could not bear the pressure. And between them stands hope, which holds everything up.

The symbolism of the same card explains the second word of the name. Waite does not call the Star the card of talent. He writes that the mottoes of this card are "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". Both go back to the New Testament, and they are easy to recognise in the Bible: "whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Revelation 22:17), "there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:4). The Russian Synodal Bible renders that "freely" — without payment — with the word darom. The Star's mottoes in Russian therefore read: "Waters of Life darom" and "Gifts of the Spirit". And dar, "gift", is the everyday Russian word for talent, much as English speaks of a "gifted" child. The card in the middle of the tail is the gift itself.

The Russian darom has two meanings: "free of charge" and "in vain" — exactly like the English "for nothing". The water of life that the Star pours out for nothing can also run out for nothing — "time spent for nothing", "all that work for nothing". **A ruined talent is a gift that went for nothing.** Not an absence of ability, but an ability that keeps draining away: given out, put off, buried.

One more detail. In all three cards of the tail Waite finds the same motif — youth and untouchedness. His Lovers are "youth, virginity, innocence and love before it is contaminated by gross material desire". The Star is "eternal youth and beauty". Strength he connects with innocentia inviolata, "inviolate innocence". The tail is made of three images of something young and unspoiled. The gift in it risks staying eternally young — which is to say, never growing up.

sections.h2: The Star in the middle: the water of life, for nothing
paragraphs: On Waite's card a naked woman kneels with one knee on the land and her other foot on the water, pouring from two jugs: one into a pool, the other onto dry ground. Waite writes that she is "irrigating sea and land" and communicates to the living scene "the substance of the heavens". The Star hoards nothing. Her action is to pour out.

Wen calls it a card of "divine charity": a person who "shares generously with others, especially of the Seeker's spiritual resources and intuitive knowledge", and who gives "more than the Seeker receives". In a reading this is good news. In the mechanism of the tail it describes how the gift drains away.

What follows is our reading. In 6-17-11 the Star keeps the loop going because the gift always finds somewhere to spill. Someone else's text that needs fixing. Someone else's project that will not take off without this person. Someone else's wedding where they are the host, and someone else's presentation where they made all the slides. A friend who needs help believing in themselves. The Star of this tail is generous and genuinely gifted, but it mostly waters other people's gardens. Its own pool — the one the second jug pours into — stays empty.

The second way the gift leaks is hope. Waite treats it almost with contempt: "The summary of several tawdry explanations says that it is a card of hope." The Russian language hints at why he is right. Of someone who has the gift but not yet the work, Russians say podayot nadezhdy — "shows promise", literally "hands out hopes". Hands out, the way the Star hands out water. While a talent is showing promise, nobody judges it strictly: everything lies ahead. **Hope is talent in the future tense, and it is a very comfortable place to live.** The trouble is that the future tense has no natural exit. At twenty, "shows promise" sounds like praise; at forty, like a reproach.

This mechanism has a well-studied side. In 1998 the psychologists Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck gave fifth-graders a set of problems and then praised some of the children for their intelligence ("you must be smart at these problems") and others for their effort. The children praised for intelligence later more often chose easier tasks — the kind where you do not risk looking less able — and gave up faster after a failure. Praising the gift turned the gift into something that had to be guarded. That is the Star of the 6-17-11 tail in everyday clothes. Once "the talented one" becomes a role, risking the role feels more frightening than burying the talent.

What is the same in every version: the water never disappears. The Star does not run dry. The question of the tail is not whether there is a gift, but where it is poured and whether even one jug is left for one's own pool.

sections.h2: The Lovers at the entry: a gift born in someone's eyes
paragraphs: Waite calls the Lovers "the card of human love". Beneath a winged figure stand a man and a woman, like Adam and Eve in paradise, "unveiled before each other". Their image, Waite writes, suggests "youth, virginity, innocence and love before it is contaminated by gross material desire". The old pictures that showed a man between vice and virtue he removed from the deck, calling them "the later follies".

Wen disagrees with him. For her, "in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice". She recalls Kierkegaard and his Either/Or: a choice between two paths in life, "either one willfully hedonistic or one grounded in our sense of ethical duty". In the Marseille deck, which the matrix follows for its numbering, this card shows a young man between two women, and interpreters still argue about who they are: virtue and vice, or mother and bride.
For 6-17-11 this argument is not a bookish detail but a description of the entry. The gift in this tail enters life by both paths at once.

The first path is Waite's love. Talent almost never begins in solitude. First someone notices it: a mother listening to her child sing; a teacher who kept the pupil back after class; a person next to whom you first wanted to write. Two people unveiled before each other. The gift is born in someone's eyes, and those eyes are loving.

There is nothing wrong with such an entry. In 1985 the educational researcher Benjamin Bloom published a study of 120 people who had reached world level in six fields — from concert pianists and sculptors to swimmers and mathematicians. In their stories the first teacher was usually not the strictest but the warmest person, someone with whom lessons were a joy. As early as the 1920s the philosopher Alfred North Whitehead called the first stage of all learning the stage of romance: first you fall in love with the subject; precision comes later.

The failure begins when the gift remains a matter between two people. If talent is what you are loved for, it cannot be risked on failure: with it, you risk the love. If talent is what the beloved values most, it starts living for one pair of eyes. Waite writes that the Star figure communicates to those below "in the measure that they can receive her influx". Our reading: **a gift poured into one cup shrinks to the size of that cup.**

The second path is Wen's choice. Kierkegaard's either/or sounds mundane in the life of this tail: either music or a proper profession; either your own work or the family; either me or us. The Lovers put the gift in one pan of the scales, love and duty in the other, and the choice seems moral: choosing the people close to you means doing the right thing. But Waite removed the picture of a man between vice and virtue from the deck. Our reading of that correction is a hint for the tail: the fork "the gift or love" is largely false. On his card the two people stand side by side, not on different roads.

sections.h2: Strength at the root: a lion on a chain of flowers
paragraphs: On Waite's card a woman is closing a lion's jaws. Waite stresses how his design differs from the conventional ones: "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers". In one aspect, Waite writes, the lion signifies the passions, and the woman is "the higher nature in its liberation".

He explains the chain of flowers as "the sweet yoke and the light burden of Divine Law, when it has been taken into the heart of hearts". The phrase echoes the Gospel: "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Matthew 11:30). Strength holds the lion not with iron and not with shouting. She holds it with what she loves.

For a tail about talent this is the most precise image of all. The lion is the very energy of the gift: hunger for the work, delight, impatience, passion for one's own thing. It cannot be killed — the gift would go with it. It cannot be let off the leash either — it would devour time, money and the patience of those nearby and still produce nothing. It can be led. **The chain of flowers is a discipline you chose yourself and are not ashamed to love:** an hour at the instrument every day, a page a day, a training session that is not cancelled because of a bad mood.

Waite has one more detail that sounds almost like a hint for 6-17-11. He recalls an early version of the card printed by Court de Gébelin in the eighteenth century: there the woman is not closing the lion's mouth — "she is obviously opening it". Waite considers the closing gesture better symbolically, but admits that either one "conveys the idea of mastery". A tail about a gift needs both. Strength decides not only when to fall silent but when to open one's mouth: to show, to sing, to sign, to go on stage. Mastery over the lion is mastery over its jaws in both directions.

Waite makes a point of saying that the card "has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense". That matters for a tail that people like to answer with the advice "believe in yourself". Strength is not a feeling about oneself. It is an action that is repeated.

Wen says the same thing more practically. For her, Strength is "domination over the Seeker's fears" (remember the servant in the parable: "I was afraid"). And in her reading of reversed Strength there is a passage that sounds like a direct description of a ruined talent: "The Seeker is holding back, and as a result is unable to achieve his or her objective. The Seeker must exercise full force of strength to prevail."

Strength also has an older name — Fortitude. Waite reminds us that it is "one of the cardinal virtues". Thomas Aquinas distinguished two acts of fortitude: to undertake (aggredi) and to endure (sustinere) — and held the second to be the principal one. For 6-17-11 this is the key to the root. Undertaking is something the gift can do: the Lovers provide the impulse, the Star the inspiration. What is missing is the other thing — enduring the third month, the hundredth rehearsal, the first bad review, the dull middle of any large piece of work. **The root task of the tail is not to find the talent but to endure it.**

In Waite's divinatory list Strength means "Power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity", followed by "also complete success and honours". A buried talent never receives honours, on principle: to receive them, the work has to be shown under one's own name. In the same list reversed Strength includes "weakness" and "despotism". Both shadows are familiar to this tail. Weakness is a gift that does not dare. Despotism is a gift that torments: perfectionism under which no piece of work is ever good enough to leave the drawer.

The three cards of the tail are three ways of handling the same gift. The Lovers show it to another person. The Star pours it out. Strength holds it. The loop turns when the first two actions are there and the third is not.

**1. Entry: the Lovers — the gift is noticed.** The occasion can be anything: someone admired, loved, chose — or set a condition. From this moment the gift becomes part of a relationship: it is used to please, to hold on to someone, it is given up for the sake of loved ones. The inner phrase of the entry is "for you" or "for your sake".

**2. Mechanism: the Star — the gift pours out.** Then it spills into everything nearby: other people's projects, help, charm, conversations about the future. The person shines, and the shine is real. But the water drains into someone else's land and into hope. The inner phrase is "later", "someday", "what matters is that people like it".

**3. Failure: Strength does not take the lion in hand.** A moment comes when the gift needs not inspiration but fortitude: long, dull work, an honest assessment, a name on the cover. Here the person holds back. Not out of laziness, but because stepping into the light puts at risk everything that rested on another person's gaze: love, the reputation of being "able", hope.

**4. Centre: Death — the gift is buried.** The loop returns to the comfort zone. "It wasn't serious", "no time for that", "I'm doing fine as it is". The gift did not die — it was buried, as in the parable. Life runs smoothly; in Waite's list for reversed Death this state is called "Inertia, sleep, lethargy, petrifaction".
**5. A new turn.** Time passes, and a new person appears: a new love, a new teacher, one's own child. Someone notices the gift again — and everything starts over with the Lovers.

Wen notes that in the deck "The Star card appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower", and indicates "that the final low point in a situation has passed". In a reading that is a comfort. In the tail it is an exact description of the rhythm. After every burial of the gift a new hope arrives, and hope keeps the loop going again.

The method's arithmetic shows what the Star of this tail is made of. The middle of the tail is the sum of the root and the entry, N = D + M. For many tails this sum has to be folded. For 6-17-11 it does not: 11 + 6 = 17. The Star here is literally the sum of Strength and the Lovers, with nothing left over.

Pushkin wrote a whole tragedy about this sum. His Salieri is outraged that "the sacred gift, / Immortal genius, is not sent as a reward / For burning love, for selflessness, / For labour, diligence and prayer — / But lights the head of a madman, / An idle reveller" (our translation). Salieri is sure the gift should be made of love and labour. In the arithmetic of the tail he is right — 17 = 6 + 11. In the picture on the card the truth is on Mozart's side: the Star pours the water for nothing and asks no one whether they deserve it. **The gift is given for nothing, but it is held by a sum.** Without the Lovers it has no life, without Strength no form. The 6-17-11 tail keeps turning as long as the second term is missing from that sum.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: Death at the centre — or the Fool
paragraphs: For nine out of ten owners of 6-17-11 the centre of the matrix is 13 — Death. For the rest it is 22, the Fool. This is not a coincidence but arithmetic: from the sums 38, 47 and 56 the centre always comes out as 13, from the sum 11 as 22. The entry of the tail is calculated from the centre, and both roads lead to the Lovers: 11 + 13 = 24 → 6 and 11 + 22 = 33 → 6.

In the method the centre of the chart is the comfort zone: the state a person returns to when nothing is demanded of them. For a tail about a gift, Death in the comfort zone sounds grim, but accurate. The safest place for a talent is the ground. A buried gift cannot be criticised, compared or rejected; it is in no danger of failing. The servant in the parable probably slept better than the others.

In the Marseille deck the thirteenth card bears no title; it is known as l'arcane sans nom, "the nameless arcanum". Our reading: the comfort zone of this tail is namelessness. Unsigned work, an idea handed to the boss, a text "on behalf of the department", a co-authorship with one's name in last place. Not because modesty is a virtue, but because without a name nothing hurts.

Waite describes his horseman like this: he "moves slowly", "carries no visible weapon, but king and child and maiden fall before him". The reversed list for Death reads "Inertia, sleep, lethargy, petrifaction, somnambulism" and, separately, "hope destroyed". The Star in the middle of the tail is hope; Death at the centre is its end. This is how the loop swings: from "someday" to "never" and back.

But Waite's Death has another side. He sees the card's main meaning in "change, transformation and passage from lower to higher". The horseman's black banner bears the Mystic Rose, "which signifies life", and on the horizon, between two pillars, shines "the sun of immortality". Wen adds that sun symbolism in the tarot can represent the "Great Work," a Seeker's magnum opus, and the rider is "marching in the direction of the rising sun, though that sun is still far in the distance".

For talent, Death has an entirely peaceful job — crossing things out. Chekhov wrote to his brother in 1889: "Brevity is the sister of talent." Editing, cutting the excess, the ability to put a full stop — these are small deaths without which no piece of work is ever finished. The comfort zone of this tail can bury the gift, or it can refine it. The difference is a single one — what exactly is being ended: the work or the attempt.

The Fool at the centre falls to one owner of the tail in ten — and to more than half of those born after 2000. Waite sees him as "the spirit in search of experience", "a prince of the other world on his travels through this one". Wen puts it more bluntly: "It is about power, but no product." In Waite's divinatory list the Fool has "extravagance", and reversed, "apathy, nullity, vanity". With the Fool at the centre of 6-17-11 the gift is not buried — it is begun. Again and again: a new instrument, a new course, a new project, each time with the delight of the first day.

The comfort zone of such a person is the eternal beginning, where nothing can fail because nothing has yet been done. Salieri would have called such a person an "idle reveller", and there would be some envy in the grudge: the Fool is at least free. His strong version is the lightness with which he takes on something new. His weak version is a gift that never reaches the end of a single road.

sections.h2: Five faces of a ruined talent

head: Face
Where the gift goes
What the person tells themselves
How it ends
rows: into other people's projects and success
"what matters is that it worked out for them"
someone else's honours and one's own emptiness
into the ground: a "proper" profession, a "childish hobby"
a smooth life and envy of those who took the risk
into the image of talent instead of the work
severity towards others' work and an empty drawer of one's own
a hundred first chapters and not one last chapter
into work under one's own name — and into others
"I do this because it is mine"

paragraphs: Many people with 6-17-11 recognise not one face but a succession of them. At twenty, the promising one; at thirty, someone else's muse; at forty, the buried; and in between, short flashes of the eternal beginner.

The least visible face is **Someone Else's Muse**. This person does not feel like a failure: they are needed, valued, indispensable. Their gift works at full power — only the signature under the result belongs to someone else. In 1968 the sociologist Robert Merton gave the name "the Matthew effect" to the way recognition in science flows to those who are already famous, while the contribution of less visible co-authors dissolves. He took the name from the same chapter about the talents: "For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance". Someone Else's Muse lives inside this effect — on the losing side.

**The Star Complex** is the flip side of the same tail, Waite's reversed Star: "Arrogance, haughtiness". The gift turns into status. The person knows they are talented, and that knowledge is enough for them. They judge other people's work strictly and do not show their own: work that is shown might turn out worse than the reputation. It is the same fear as the servant's in the parable, only in an expensive suit.

**The Buried** often does not think about the tail at all. Everything is fine for them, and that is true. The gift reminds them of itself in other ways: a sudden anger at someone else's success in their former field, tears at a concert, a heavy silence when their child quits music school. The ground in which the talent lies is not as deaf as it seems.

sections.h2: The tail in the mirror: where else 6, 17 and 11 appear in the chart
paragraphs: The 6-17-11 triple does not live only on the lower ray of the matrix. Going through every date from 1900 to 2026 shows where else it appears and what all its owners have in common.

**The relationship line always begins with the Lovers.** Point M, the entry of the tail, is shared in the method with the relationship line M–R1–R. So for every owner of 6-17-11 the relationship line opens with card 6. And for those born in years whose digits add up to 19 — 1909, 1918, 1927 and so on every nine years up to 1990 — and in 1999, 2008, 2017 and 2026, the relationship line repeats the tail digit for digit: 6-17-11. That is 13% of the tail's owners, almost one in seven. For them the scenario of the gift and the scenario of the couple are one and the same sequence.

**For those born in November the tail is mirrored in the talent line.** The month number stands at the start of the talent line B–P–K on the upper ray of the chart. For November-born owners of 6-17-11 it reads 11-17-6 — the same tail backwards. The tail known as the ruined talent is written into their talent line literally, only from the root to the entry. One owner in eight is like this. Our reading: on the upper ray the task is the same, but the road runs the other way. First hold (Strength), then pour (the Star), then share (the Lovers).

**The entry of the tail sits in the chakra of creativity.** Two cards of the tail appear in the chakra table of every owner. The Lovers stand in Svadhisthana, in the energy column; Strength in Muladhara, also in energy. The product describes Svadhisthana as "joy, children, creativity" and Muladhara as "body, support, matter". The entry of the tail falls exactly into the chakra of creativity, the root into the chakra of support. The Star is not in the table: the method does not place the middle of the tail in the chakras.

**In Manipura everyone has the same emotions.** In the Manipura row ("status, will, money") the centre appears twice — 13 and 13, or 22 and 22 — and the total in the emotions column is the same for all: 8, Justice (13 + 13 = 26 → 8, 22 + 22 = 44 → 8). Our reading: in matters of money and status this tail always carries the question of a fair price. Will the work be valued as it deserves? Is what pours out for nothing being paid for honestly?
The scenes below are illustrative examples, not a description of every person with this tail.

**The only spectator.** The gift lives for one pair of eyes. The person sings, writes, draws while their partner admires it — and stops when the relationship ends or the delight fades into habit. The partner becomes muse, jury and audience all at once. No one can carry three roles, and the gift becomes hostage to the couple's mood.

**For your sake.** This is the plot of the choice: "either the stage or the family", "either the move to the big city or Mum left alone". People choose their loved ones, and in the moment this is often the right choice. The trouble begins later, when the sacrifice turns into a bill: "I had to give up everything for you". The loved ones never asked for such a sacrifice, and the person feels for years that they paid for nothing — in both senses of the phrase.

**A muse for someone else.** The person picks a partner who shines brighter and invests their own gift in that partner's success: editing the texts, running the social media, keeping the house while the other creates. Exactly the Star watering someone else's land.

The strong version in all three plots is **a witness instead of a judge**. The gift needs the person close by as a witness: to see that the work is going on, to be glad, to support. Assessment is better sought elsewhere — from a master, from the audience, from the market. And time for the work is agreed on in the family as working time, not as a whim.

The strong side here is real: taste, charm, the ability to inspire, a feel for what people will like. People with 6-17-11 are good at lighting a spark in others — a team, students, clients, an audience.

The first shadow is working for nothing. The Star of this tail easily does for free what others get paid for: "oh, it's no trouble". The second is the eternal "promising employee" who has been promised a project of their own for three years. The third is a profession as a shelter: a safe place where the gift is not needed, which means nothing to be afraid of.

Things go well where giving is the job itself, but for money and under one's own name: teaching, mentoring, editing, producing, design, the stage, a service in which charm is a professional skill. And where the gift has a chain of flowers: regularity, deadlines, a master who makes demands.

The most common family form of this tail is passing the ruined gift on to the children. Music school "because I never got the chance", the trips to competitions, nerves louder than the child's own. The Star once again pours water onto someone else's land — this time the land of one's own child, who has been handed someone else's unplayed part.

The second form is praising talent. The Mueller and Dweck experiment shows where it leads: the child starts guarding the label of "able" and avoiding tasks where it could be lost. A parent with 6-17-11 does better to praise the work rather than the gift: "you spent a long time on it and figured it out", not "you're my little genius".

Among children born after 2000 the tail more often comes with the Fool at the centre. For these children the eternal beginning comes easily: club after club, enthusiasm after enthusiasm. What they need is not an iron chain — "you started it, so you finish it" — but a chain of flowers: a small but steady rhythm in something they chose themselves.

sections.h2: Gift or label: how to tell a living talent from a ruined one

ul: Does "someday" have a date, a scope and a first step this week?
What has changed over the past year in the work itself — not in the plans for it?
Does "shows promise" still sound like praise — or already like a postponement?
After helping others, is there time and energy left for one's own work — or is one's own work always "later"?
Does one's own work grow alongside other people's — or do theirs grow instead of it?
Does anyone know the author's name next to the result?
Who sees the work first — the one who will be glad, or the one who will pass judgement?
Does the work go on when the person close by is indifferent or in a quarrel?
Has one person become muse, judge and the entire audience all at once?

paragraphs.h3: A chain of flowers or a whip

ul: Does the discipline rest on love of the work — or on fear and shame?
Is it possible to miss a day without self-reproach and come back tomorrow?
Does perfectionism help to finish — or stop the work from being shown?

sections.h2: What to do with the 6-17-11 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: These are the author's exercises derived from the logic of the triple — not a ritual and not a promise of results. Each one targets its own link in the loop: the entry, the mechanism, the root or the centre.

ol: **The second jug.** The Star pours from two jugs, and one of them is your own. Set aside time for your own work that is not given away to other people's requests: an hour in the morning before other people's tasks, one evening a week, a free day once a month. Your own pool first, then someone else's land.

**A chain of flowers.** Not a vow of "three hours a day starting Monday", but a small rhythm you enjoy: fifteen minutes at the instrument, half a page, one sketch. The chain must be light — Waite says as much: "the light burden". A heavy one will snap in the second week.
**Show the unfinished.** Against the Star that guards the reputation of being "able". Once a month, show work in progress to someone who knows the field, and ask for a critique, not praise.

**Sign it.** Against the centre where the card has no name. Finish one thing and release it under your own name: a post, an exhibition in a café, a performance at an open mic, a piece in your portfolio. In Waite's lists the honours belong to Strength, not to the Star: they go to the one who holds, not to the one who shows promise.
**The price of water.** Stop doing for nothing what is actually work. Name a price in at least one case out of three. Free help remains — but as a gift by decision, not as a habit.

**A witness, not a jury.** Agree with the person close to you: what you need from them is support, not assessment. Get assessment from a master, from an audience, from the market. That way the gift stops being hostage to the relationship.

**Small deaths.** Use the centre for its proper purpose: every month, end something deliberately. Finish it or honestly close it, cross out the excess, drop one of five started projects in order to complete the rest. "Brevity is the sister of talent" is also about death — only a peaceful one.

**Your own for yourself, theirs for the children.** If your own gift has not been lived, do not hand it to your children as an assignment. Let music school be chosen by the one who will study there. The best way not to ruin someone else's talent is not to bury your own.

paragraphs: If the feeling that "it all went for nothing" turns into a long heaviness, with sleep and interest in everything slipping away, that is a reason to see a psychologist or a doctor, not to reread the analysis of the tail.

sections.h2: The strong side of 6-17-11: the gift in your own hands
paragraphs: In its lived-through version this tail produces a rare combination. The person can love and be open (the Lovers), share generously what they can do and light a spark in others (the Star) — and at the same time keep their own work in their own hands, for a long time and calmly (Strength). They resemble a teacher who still plays; an editor who also publishes books of their own; a performer who runs a studio. The water pours from both jugs: onto other people's land and into one's own pool.

Wen writes of the Star that "Guidance is not coming from others, but rather it is coming from within". That is the shift a lived-through 6-17-11 makes. The gift was born in someone else's eyes, but it is held from within. The eyes of loved ones remain — as a joy, not as a condition.

There is also an unexpected consolation for the Star that waters other people's gardens. The real Antonio Salieri, despite the legend of the poisoning, was no envious failure. He was a celebrated composer and one of the most influential teachers of his time: Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt studied with him. A gift given to students is not ruined if it is given under one's own name and by one's own decision. What ruins it is not generosity, but generosity that has become a way of not doing one's own work.

Waite's Strength card shows how this tail ends in its best version. The lion is neither killed nor escaped. It is being led, and the chain of flowers does not break, because it does not have to be held by force. This is what a gift looks like when it has stopped being a hope and become a body of work.

sections.h2: What this analysis is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme of Natalia Ladini with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M; every sum greater than 22 is folded by adding its digits. All numerical facts in the article — the four sums, the two possible centres, the frequencies by generation and month, the repetition of the triple in the relationship and talent lines, the chakra rows — come from going through every date from 01.01.1900 to 05.10.2026.

**Waite** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; 1922 reprint): the symbolism of the Lovers, the Star, Strength, Death and the Fool (Part II), the divinatory meanings (Part III), early designs (Part I). Quotations are from the original.
**Wen** — Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), chapter 9: the Lovers, the Star, Strength, Death, the Fool. Quotations are from the original.

**The Bible** — the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30), "my yoke is easy" (Matthew 11:30), "the water of life freely" (Revelation 22:17), "diversities of gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:4) — in the King James Version.

**Literature and philosophy** — A. S. Pushkin, Mozart and Salieri (1830); A. P. Chekhov, letter to his brother Alexander (1889); Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae (II-II, question 123); S. Kierkegaard, Either/Or (1843); A. N. Whitehead, The Rhythm of Education (1922).

**Psychology and sociology** — B. S. Bloom (ed.), Developing Talent in Young People (1985); C. M. Mueller, C. S. Dweck, Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance (1998); R. K. Merton, The Matthew Effect in Science (1968).
**Popular interpretations** — the past-life legend and the variants of the name are retold from openly published destiny matrix readings. They cannot be verified.

**Our reading** — the mechanism of the loop, the five faces, the meaning of the centre, the reading of the lines and chakras, the practices. This is an author's interpretation within an esoteric system, not an established fact.

paragraphs: For a couple, 6-17-11 is the task of supporting each other’s growth without chasing an image of the perfect couple. Here the Lovers are the entry to the task, the Star is its middle, and Strength is the main task: respect for what each person can do and a sense of measure in the load.

faq.q: What happened in a past life to someone with the 6-17-11 tail?
faq.a: Popular readings say that in a past incarnation the person had a bright gift and did not realise it: gave it up for a steady income or a family, grew proud and fell, could not bear the criticism. This cannot be verified: the numbers of the matrix say nothing about past lives. What can be verified is something else — that this scenario is written into the cards themselves. The middle card of the tail, the Star, opens Waite's divinatory list with the words "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment", and the reversed card has "Arrogance, haughtiness, impotence".

faq.q: Does 6-17-11 mean there is no talent, or that it will never unfold?
faq.a: No. The tail predicts neither success nor failure and does not measure ability. If anything, the opposite: in the middle of the tail stands the Star, the card of the gift, which Waite connects with the mottoes "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". The tail's scenario is not about a lack of talent but about where the gift drains away: into other people's projects, into the hope of "someday", into the ground. The numbers do not change; the way the gift is handled does.

If 11, 17 and 6 stand on the lower ray of the chart — yes, the tail has simply been read from the outer corner towards the centre. The method writes it from the inner point M to the corner D. But the same triple in reverse order can also appear elsewhere: for every owner of 6-17-11 born in November, the talent line B–P–K reads 11-17-6. This is not a second tail but a reflection of the same scenario on the upper ray.

faq.q: Why is 11 Strength here, when tarot books make Strength card 8?
faq.a: These are two numberings of the deck. In the old Marseille deck the eighth card is Justice and the eleventh is Strength, and the destiny matrix counts in that order. Waite swapped the two cards and only wrote that he did so "for reasons which satisfy myself". The meaning of a card rests on its name and image, not its number: the Strength at the root of 6-17-11 is the woman with the lion under any numbering.

It shares its entry with 6-5-17 — the Lovers — and both contain the Star. But in 6-5-17 the Star stands at the root, and the middle is the Hierophant — rule, tradition, someone else's norm. It shares its root with 15-8-11 — Strength — but the entry and mechanism are different: the Devil and Justice, anger and verdict rather than a gift. In 6-17-11 the Star is the mechanism: the gift here is not a goal to strive towards but water that keeps draining away. The tails also differ by sum: 6-17-11 comes from the sums 11, 38, 47 and 56, while 15-8-11 comes only from 29.

faq.q: Is 6-17-11 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Sex plays no part in the calculation and does not change the tail's meaning. Popular readings like to write that for women this tail means a life of waiting and self-sacrifice, and for men softness and indecision. These are stereotypes, not arithmetic. Giving your gift away to a partner, children or an employer, burying it for the sake of stability, forever showing promise — all of this is equally open to people of any sex.

There are fewer such children now: among those born after 2000 the tail falls to roughly one in forty-odd, and for more than half of them the centre is the Fool, not Death. The main thing is not to turn the gift into a label. Praise the work and the effort, not the "ability". Do not pass on your own unplayed dream to the child. Help them keep a small steady rhythm in something they chose themselves, and be a witness to their practice, not a jury.

In this method the karmic tail is personal: it is calculated from a single date and describes one person's scenario. Compatibility is calculated differently, and some forum lists of "compatibility tails" call the same set of numbers "Wicked Love" — that is a different system. For a couple something else matters more: for every owner of 6-17-11 the relationship line begins with the Lovers, and for some it matches the tail completely. That is why their gift so easily starts living for a partner.

The numbers in the matrix do not change — what changes is how the scenario plays out. Signs of a tail that has been lived through: one's own work has a fixed time that is not given away to other people's requests; the work leaves the drawer under one's own name; helping others is a gift by decision, not a habit; masters and audiences give the assessment, while loved ones remain witnesses. And "someday" has been replaced by a deadline.

report: The servant in the Gospel parable did not lose his talent, nor did he squander it. He was afraid. That is exactly what he tells his master: "And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine." It was from this parable that the word "talent" took on the meaning of "ability". And from the same parable grows the name of the 6-17-11 tail — the "Ruined Talent".

Popular readings tell a legend about a past life: the soul had a bright gift and never put it to work. It gave the gift up for a steady income or for family, grew proud and fell, could not stand the mockery and hid it away. The legend cannot be checked: the numbers say nothing about past lives. But every plot of it is written into a single card, and that card stands in the middle of the tail.

report.h3: What stands in the middle of the tail is not a void but a gift

report: The middle card of 6-17-11 is the Star. In Waite's divinatory list its first words are "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment", and only then comes "another reading says—hope and bright prospects". For the reversed Star Waite gives "Arrogance, haughtiness, impotence". Giving up the calling, pride, powerlessness under pressure — the whole legend fits into one list.

Yet the symbolism of the same card says the main thing: the gift is there. Waite gives the Star's mottoes as "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". In the Bible these words appear as "the water of life freely" and "diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit", and the Russian Bible renders that "freely" with the word darom — which, like the English "for nothing", means both "free of charge" and "in vain". **A ruined talent is a gift that went for nothing.** Not an absence of ability, but an ability that keeps draining away: given out, put off, buried.

report.h3: The water pours onto someone else's land and into the future tense

report: The Lovers (6) open the loop. Waite calls them "the card of human love", Wen sees a moral choice in them, and the gift of this tail enters life by both paths. Someone close notices it — a mother, a teacher, a beloved — and the talent becomes part of a relationship: it is used to please, to hold on to someone. Or a fork is set in front of it: either music or a proper profession; either one's own work or the family. A gift poured into one cup shrinks to the size of that cup.

The Star (17) keeps the loop going. On Waite's card she pours water from two jugs and hoards nothing. In our reading the gift here always finds somewhere to spill: someone else's text that needs fixing, someone else's project that will not take off without this person. The second way it leaks is hope. Of someone who has the gift but not yet the work, people say they "show promise". **Hope is talent in the future tense, and it is a very comfortable place to live.** At twenty, "shows promise" sounds like praise; at forty, like a reproach.

In 1998 the psychologists Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck praised some fifth-graders for their intelligence and others for their effort. Those praised for intelligence later more often chose easier tasks and gave up faster after a failure. Once "the talented one" becomes a role, risking the role feels more frightening than burying the talent.

report.h3: The safest place for a talent is the ground

report: The loop closes at the centre of the chart, and in the method the centre is the comfort zone. With this tail it holds Death or, less often, the Fool. A buried gift cannot be criticised or rejected. In the Marseille deck the thirteenth card bears no title; it is known as "the nameless arcanum", and the comfort zone of the tail, in our reading, is namelessness: unsigned work, an idea handed to the boss. Waite's reversed list for Death reads "Inertia, sleep, lethargy, petrifaction, somnambulism" and, separately, "hope destroyed". This is how the loop swings: from "someday" to "never" and back. Where the Fool is at the centre, the gift is not buried but forever begun — each time with the delight of the first day.
Then a new person appears: a new love, a new teacher, one's own child. Someone notices the gift again, and everything starts over with the Lovers.

report.h3: The gift is given for nothing, but it is held by a sum

report: The Star of this tail is literally made of its two other cards: its number is the sum of the numbers of Strength and the Lovers. Pushkin's Salieri was outraged that "the sacred gift" is "not sent as a reward / For burning love, for selflessness, / For labour, diligence and prayer". In the arithmetic of the tail he is right. In the picture on the card the truth is on Mozart's side: the Star pours the water for nothing. **The gift is given for nothing, but it is held by a sum.** Without the Lovers it has no life, without Strength no form.

At the root stands Strength (11). On Waite's card a woman leads a lion on a chain of flowers, and Waite explains the chain as "the sweet yoke and the light burden of Divine Law, when it has been taken into the heart of hearts". The lion is the energy of the gift. It cannot be killed, nor let off the leash; it can be led. Waite makes a point of saying that the card "has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense". Thomas Aquinas distinguished two acts of fortitude — to undertake and to endure — and held the second to be the principal one. Undertaking is something the gift of this tail can do. **The root task is not to find the talent but to endure it.**

report.h3: One of the two jugs is one's own

report: The way out is not to stop giving. The Star pours from two jugs, and one of them belongs to oneself: time for one's own work that is not given away to other people's requests. The chain must be light — fifteen minutes at the instrument, half a page, one sketch; a heavy one will snap in the second week. The gift needs the person close by as a witness, not a jury. Finish one thing and release it under one's own name. Stop doing for nothing what is actually work.
If the feeling that "it all went for nothing" turns into a long heaviness, with sleep and interest in everything slipping away, that is a reason to see a psychologist or a doctor.

The real Antonio Salieri, despite the legend of the poisoning, was no envious failure: Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt studied with him. What ruins a gift is not generosity, but generosity that has become a way of not doing one's own work. The lion on the Strength card is neither killed nor escaped. It is being led, and the chain of flowers does not break, because it does not have to be held by force.
